_comment: Further stories cut from the newly supplied Evelyn-White (1914, public domain) editions of Hesiod: full Theogony, Works and Days, and the Shield of Heracles. All passages are paraphrase with notes.

title.en: Heracles, the Wonderful Shield, and the Death of Cycnus
title.zh: 赫拉克勒斯神盾與刻克努斯之死

region.en: Grove of Apollo at Pagasae, Thessaly (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 色薩利帕加薩阿波羅聖林（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Composed c. 6th century BCE (?), attributed to Hesiod (Evelyn-White translation 1914)

source.work: Ps.-Hesiod, Shield of Heracles, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White (1914), lines ca. 1-480

summary.en: Zeus comes by night to Alcmene, Amphitryon's faithful wife, while her husband is away burning the villages of the Taphians; she bears twins — Iphicles to her mortal husband, Heracles to the god. Years later Heracles and his charioteer Iolaus face Cycnus, the cruel son of Ares, and Ares himself in Apollo's grove: the god's new-made shield, emblazoned with Fear and battle-panic, cities and weddings and the Fates clawing at the fallen, protects the hero while he spears Cycnus through the neck and wounds Ares in the thigh, and Panic and Terror drive the raging war-god screaming back to Olympus.
summary.zh: 宙斯乘夜降臨安菲特律翁貞潔之妻阿爾克墨涅，其夫正赴塔福斯征戰；她產下雙胎：伊菲克勒斯屬凡父，赫拉克勒斯屬於神。日後赫拉克勒斯與御者伊俄拉俄斯在阿波羅聖林迎戰阿瑞斯之子刻克努斯及戰神本人：神匠特製的神盾滿怖恐懼與戰慄、城邦婚禮與抓拿亡者的命運女神，護著英雄以矛貫穿刻克努斯頸項，又刺傷阿瑞斯大腿；恐慌與恐怖二神架車，把咆哮的戰神送回奧林波斯。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Alcmena, daughter of Electryon, came to Thebes as the wife of Amphitryon, who had fled Tiryns after killing her father in a quarrel over oxen, and went suppliant to the shield-bearing men of Cadmus; until he had avenged her brothers and burned the villages of the Taphians and Teleboans, he might not go in to his wife, and the gods stood witness to the bargain. But Zeus, father of gods and men, was weaving another plan: to beget a defender who would keep both gods and bread-eating men from ruin. So one night he came down from Olympus and lay with Alcmene; and that same night her husband too, home from his heavy task, lay with her, rejoicing like a man escaped out of sickness or chains.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shield of Heracles, lines ca. 1-56 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: She bore two sons in seven-gated Thebes, brothers unlike in spirit: Iphicles, weaker, of Amphitryon's fathering; and the terrible strong Heracles, the joy of Zeus of the dark clouds. Years on, with Alcmena's son grown, Zeus showered gifts upon him: the practice of killing Cycnus, the gallant son of Ares, in the close-grown grove of far-shooting Apollo — father and son stood in a chariot with armour like blazing fire, dust about their wheels; Cycnus wished aloud to strip their splendid armour, but Phoebus Apollo, who had stirred Heracles against him, would not listen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shield of Heracles, lines ca. 57-88 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: Heracles armed at the grove of Apollo: greaves, a golden breastplate of Athena's giving, a hollow quiver of death-bearing arrows, a spear, a close-fitted adamant helmet — and a shield the smith-god had made for him, a marvel no blow could break: in its centre Fear, unutterable, staring backward with eyes of fire, gnashing a white row of teeth; about him Strife, and Pursuit and Flight, and Panic, and Slaughter; deadly Fate dragging a newly-wounded man and casting behind him one already dead; twelve snake-heads on the rim to terrify the foes of the son of Zeus; and then the whole world by way of interleaf: boars and lions at battle, the Lapith spearmen against the Centaurs, Ares in his chariot and the drive of spoil-winning Athena, Olympus itself with Apollo playing the lyre and the Muses beginning their song, a tin-built harbour of darting dolphins and a watchful fisherman, Perseus flying with the winged sandals and the Gorgon's head in its silver bag while the immortal Gorgons storm after him on Adamantine paths, a city of dance and torchlight and festivals, ploughmen and vintage-men and boxers and wrestler, horse-race about a golden tripod, and Ocean flowing around the whole rim of the shield with swans above and fish below.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shield of Heracles, lines ca. 139-326 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: Grey-eyed Athena came to the warriors' car and told Heracles the plan of battle: when Cycnus fell he was to leave the body and its armour, and watch only the man-slaying Ares, striking wherever he saw flesh uncovered beneath the cunning shield, then drawing back — it was not fated that he should take the god's horses or splendid armour. At her word they bore down; the earth rang; and Heracles called Cycnus to guide his car aside and yield the road, for he drove to Trachis, to Ceyx the king: already the war-god had thrice been dashed to earth by this spear at sandy Pylos, and the fourth thrust had cut his thigh and thrown him headlong. Cycnus heeded nothing: from their cars they sprang to the ground with a great shout, like two lions over a slain deer; Zeus thundered loud and rained drops of blood, the signal of battle for his dauntless son.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shield of Heracles, lines ca. 327-401 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: Cycnus cast his brazen spear and could not break the bronze; but Heracles struck him in the neck beneath the chin, where the throat lies unguarded between helmet and shield, and the two sinews were cut through; Cycnus fell like a tall pine hit by Zeus's thunderbolt, his armour clashing about him. Then Ares came at him with grief for his dead son: he hurled his spear at the great shield, and Athena turned its force aside; and when the god drew his sword and leapt upon the son of Amphitryon, Heracles shrewdly wounded his bare thigh under the richly-wrought shield and tore deep into the flesh, and dashed him flat on the ground. Swiftly Panic and Terror drew near and lifted Ares into his chariot and lashed the horses to high Olympus. So Heracles and Iolaus stripped the armour from the dead Cycnus and drove their horses to Trachis; and Ceyx buried the fallen man — though a rain-swollen Anaurus later, on Apollo's orders, blotted out his grave and memorial, because he had been a plunderer of the rich hecatombs brought to Pytho.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shield of Heracles, lines ca. 402-480 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

region.zh: 波厄提亞阿斯克拉村（赫西俄德故鄉，象徵性定位）

source.work: Hesiod, Theogony, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White (1914), lines ca. 211-232

summary.en: Born without a bedfellow, black Night brought forth the kindred of mortal fear: Doom, Death, Sleep and Dreams, the Hesperides, Blame and Woe, the Fates and the death-spirits, Nemesis, Deceit, Friendship, Old Age, and last of all Strife — whose own children are Toil, Forgetfulness, Hunger, Pains, Battles, Murders, Quarrels, Lies, Lawlessness, and Oath.
summary.zh: 黑夜無偶而生：命運、死亡、睡與夢、赫斯珀里得斯、譴責與悲苦、命運三女神與報應女神、欺瞞與友愛、老邁，最後是紛爭——紛爭復生勞苦、遺忘、飢餓、悲苦、戰陣、凶殺、口角、謊言、無法與誓言。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Hesiod's catalogue of the divine families reaches next to Earth's dark kin. From Chaos had come Erebos and black Night; and Night, without sleeping with any god, brought forth Doom and Death and sleep herself, and the race of Dreams; she bore too the Hesperides, who tend beyond glorious Ocean the golden apples and the trees that bear them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 211-222 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: Night brought forth also the Moirai, the Fates, and the Keres, the death-spirits who pursue offenders: Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos, who give men at their birth both good and evil, and who pursue the transgressions of gods and men — the goddesses whose wrath never ceases until they have punished the sinner with a heavy penalty. And Nemesis, that evil for mortals, is Night's child also, and after her Deceit and Friendship and cruel Old Age, and, strong-hearted Strife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 217-226 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: Strife, in turn, had a brood of her own: Toil, Forgetfulness, Famine and grievous Pains; Combats, Battles, Manslaughters, Murders; Quarrels, Lying words, Disputes; Lawlessness and Ruin, all of one kin, and Oath, who brings men their greatest sorrow when they swear a false oath out of willingness. The night-brood is thus a map of the misfortunes that stalk human life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 226-232 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

region.zh: 克里特至特洛伊（神話地理）

source.work: Hesiod, Theogony, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White (1914), lines ca. 960-1018

summary.en: Now the Muses sing the race of goddesses who lay with men: Demeter with Iasion in a thrice-ploughed field, bearing Wealth; Eos with Tithonus, bearing Memnon of the gushing river Ethiope kingship; Thetis with Peleus, bearing single-hearted Achilles scatterer of men; Aphrodite with Anchises on Ida, bearing Aeneas; Circe and Calypso with Odysseus; and Medea, golden Aphrodite's kiss on Aeetes' daughter, wed to Jason.
summary.zh: 繆斯繼而歌詠與凡人交合的女神一系：得墨忒耳於三度新耕之田與伊阿西翁生財神普路托斯；厄俄斯與提托諾斯生門儂；忒提斯與珀琉斯生疏敵蕩手的阿基琉斯；阿芙洛狄忒於伊達山與安喀塞斯生埃涅阿斯；喀耳刻與卡呂普索皆戀奧德修斯；美狄亞為埃厄忒斯之女、得金劍之戀而下嫁伊阿宋。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Fair-cheeked Demeter lay with the hero Iasion in a thrice-ploughed fallow field in the fruitful land of Crete, and bore Plutus, the kindly god who walks the whole earth and the back of the sea; the man who meets him and takes him by the hand is enriched, for Wealth brims his hands with substance. And golden Aphrodite's daughter Harmonia, wed to Cadmus, bore Ino, Semele, fair-cheeked Agave, Autonoe, and Polydorus, in the fair-meadowed halls of Thebes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 963-980 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: And Eos bore to Tithonus the bronze-helmeted Memnon, king of the Aethiopians, and lord Emathion; and to Cephalus a shining son, mighty Phaethon, a god among mortal men: while he was still a delicate youth in tender flower, laughter-loving Aphrodite seized him up and made him her nightly watchman of sacred temples, a shining guardian. And by the plan of the immortal gods the strong son of Aeson, Jason, bore off from Aeetes' halls the daughter of Zeus-honoured Aeetes — after the many grievous tasks set him by the wild king — and brought her home to Iolcus by night, on the swift ship, with rosy-cheeked Medea, child of golden Aphrodite's force upon Idyia's blood-line, and wed her: she bore Medus, whom the centaur Chiron reared in the mountains.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 984-1000 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: The daughters of the Old Man of the Sea came last: subtle-minded Psamathe bore to Aeacus the great Phocus; and silver-footed Thetis, wedding Peleus, bore the lion-hearted Achilles, the scatterer of ranks. And Cyprus-born Cytherea lay with Anchises on the peaks of windy Ida with its many glens, and bore Aeneas. Circe, child of Helios, bore to the enduring Odysseus Agrius and Latinus, lordly rulers of the far Tyrrhenian isles; and Calypso, nymph of Ogygia, bore him Nausithous and Nausinous: and so the line of heroes was braided into the dynasty of the gods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 1010-1018 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

title.en: Echidna's Brood: The Womb of Monsters
title.zh: 厄喀德那的子嗣：怪物之母

region.zh: 阿里馬亞洞窟（神話地理）

source.work: Hesiod, Theogony, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White (1914), lines ca. 295-338

summary.en: In a cave beyond the reach of gods and men lives Echidna, half nymph and half raw-flesh-eating serpent, mate of Typhon. She bears Orthrus the two-headed dog, Cerberus of Hades, the Lernaean Hydra, and the fire-breathing Chimera; and the Chimera, mated to Orthrus, in turn bears the Sphinx and the Nemean lion — the whole catalogue of heroes' monsters.
summary.zh: 厄喀德那半身仙子、半身食生肉之蛇，棲於人神難至的阿斯洞穴，配堤豐而生雙首犬俄耳托斯、冥府犬刻耳柏洛斯、勒拿九頭蛇與噴火奇美拉；奇美拉再配俄耳托斯，誕下忒拜的斯芬克斯與尼米亞獅——英雄們的怪物世界由此而出。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: In a hollow cave beneath a great rock, far from immortal gods and mortal men, the gods keep the house of Echidna: a quick-glancing maiden above, a terrible snake below that eats raw flesh in hidden places under the earth. There, it is told, she lay with the violent and lawless Typhon, and, gotten with child, bore his fearsome brood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 297-308 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: Her first-born was Orthrus, the herdsman-dog of Geryon; next Cerberus, devourer of raw flesh, the bronze-voiced dog of Hades, fifty-headed, pitiless and powerful; then the Lernaean Hydra of evil heart, whom white-armed Hera reared in wrath against Heracles — but Heracles, son of Zeus, slew it too with pitiless bronze, helped by Iolaus and Athena's cunning.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 309-318 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: Echidna bore the invincible Chimera, fire-breathing, huge and swift: three heads, lion and she-goat and serpent; lion before, goat behind, serpent at the tail, flame from each. Pegasus and noble Bellerophon destroyed her. And the Chimera mated with Orthrus and brought forth the doom-laden Sphinx to spite the men of Cadmus, and the Nemean lion, bane of mortals, whom Zeus's queen Hera raised and set in the Nemean valley to lay waste the tribes of men, until the strength of Heracles overcame it too.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 319-330 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

title.en: Perseus and the Beheading of Medusa

region.en: Beyond Oceanus, lair of the Gorgons (mythic geography)
region.zh: 大洋之外，戈耳貢巢穴（神話地理）

source.work: Hesiod, Theogony, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White (1914), lines ca. 270-287

summary.en: Phorcys and Ceto bore the immortal Gorgons beyond Ocean, and of them Medusa alone was mortal. Poseidon lay with her in a flowered meadow, and when Perseus cut off her head, great Chrysaor — wielder of the golden sword — sprang out, and the horse Pegasus, who flew up to the immortals and carries the thunderbolts of Zeus.
summary.zh: 福爾庫斯與刻托在大洋之外育出不朽的戈耳貢三姊妹，唯美杜莎為可死之身。波塞頓曾與她於花間草甸交歡；珀爾修斯斬下其首後，持金劍的克律薩俄耳與神馬珀伽索斯一齊躍出，神馬飛抵不死族，為宙斯馱運雷霆。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Sea's old man Phorcys wed the deep Ceto, and their children glittered at the edge of the world: the grey-haired Graiae, sisters born with grey from the womb, and the Gorgons who dwell beyond glorious Ocean at the edge of night where the clear-voiced Hesperides keep house — Sthenno and Euryale, immortal and ageless forever, and Medusa alone of the three was mortal.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 270-281 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: The dark-haired Poseidon had lain with Medusa in a soft meadow among the spring flowers; and so when the hero Perseus cut off her head, the Gorgon's death was also a birth-opening: out of her neck came the great Chrysaor and the foal Pegasus, the one named for the gold sword he bore, the other born by the water's edge.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 277-285 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: Pegasus left the earth, mother of flocks, and flew up to the immortals: he dwells thereafter in the house of Zeus, bringing to his king the well-woven thunder and lightning that the god hurls. Chrysaor, in turn, married Callirrhoe, daughter of Ocean, and she bore him the triple-headed Geryon, whom Heracles would one day kill for his shambling cattle on the far island of Erytheia.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 283-295 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

source.work: Hesiod, Theogony, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White (1914), lines ca. 881-930

summary.en: After the wars, Zeus the king takes his wives in order, and each marriage brings an office into the settled world: Metis — whom he swallows outright, so that Athena may be born from his head; Themis, who bears the Seasons and the Fates; Eurynome the Graces; Demeter Persephone; Mnemosyne the nine Muses; Leto Apollo and Artemis; and Hera, queen and last, whose fury at Athena's head-birth brings forth Hephaestus without a father.
summary.zh: 戰事既畢，宙斯依次娶妻，每一樁婚姻都為新秩序帶來執掌：吞下智慧女神墨提斯，雅典娜自其首而出；忒彌斯生時序三女神與命運三女神；歐律諾墨生美惠三女神；得墨忒耳生珀耳塞福涅；謨涅摩敘涅生九繆斯；勒托生阿波羅與阿爾忒彌斯；末娶赫拉，竟因雅典娜降生而獨自生下赫菲斯托斯。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: First Zeus took Metis, wisest of gods and men, for his wife. But when she was on the point of bearing Athena, the crafty king talked her round, and gulped her down into his belly — for Earth and starry Heaven had warned him that Metis was fated to bear children beyond his throne: first the flashing daughter equal to her father in mind and strength, and then a son, a king of gods and men with a proud heart. Zeus swallowed the danger, and his own belly became the child's chamber.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 881-900 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: Next he wedded shining Themis, who bore the Horae — Lawfulness, Justice and blooming Peace, who watch over the works of mortal men — and the Fates, Clotho, Lachesis and Atropos, whom the cunning Zeus honoured above all, for they allot mortal men good and evil alike. Then Eurynome, child of Ocean, bore the Graces — Aglae, Euphrosyne and Thalia — whose glances loosen desire and delight the eyes; and bountiful Demeter bore gleaming-armed Persephone, whom Hades stole from her mother with the nod of Zeus.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 901-915 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Zeus loved the lovely-haired Mnemosyne, who bore the nine gold-banded Muses of Pieria, painters of laughter and sweet song; and Leto, who bore Apollo of the silver bow and Artemis of the arrow, dearest children of Heaven. Last of all he made his own flourishing queen Hera, who bore Hebe of the golden crown, Ares of the dreadful war-cry, and Eileithyia of childbed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 915-922 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: But there was no joy even in its end: when Hera saw how Zeus — and Zeus alone, without a mother in the deed — had birthed grey-eyed Athena, terrible in arms and sacker of cities, anger came into her heart, and she conceived without mingling in love, and by her own device bore Hephaestus, the craftsman whose hands surpassed every son of Heaven; and thus the smith-god entered the world god-born differently from all his kin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Theogony, lines ca. 925-930 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

title.en: Lucky Days and the Thirty Thousand Watchers

region.zh: 波厄提亞阿斯克拉村（象徵性定位）

source.work: Hesiod, Works and Days, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White (1914), lines ca. 240-285, 724-828

summary.en: The poem closes Hesiod's lesson in time: the days the gods have marked out are gods' gifts — a man must know them and teach his slaves, for the thirtieth is best for meting out rations, the first, fourth and seventh are sacred days, and none should urinate standing toward the sun nor cross a river with unpurged hands. Below it all runs the belief threaded through Works and Days: Zeus has thirty thousand watchers over men's deeds in the mist of earth, recording judgments and merciless acts.
summary.zh: 《勞作與時日》以時間之學收尾：諸神劃定的日子是神賜——須識而教僕，三十日宜分食舍，每月第一、四、七日為聖日；人們不該面向太陽撒尿，亦不可未洗手便過河。而貫穿全詩的信念是：宙斯派駐人間的三萬守望神，在塵霧中記錄每一樁審判與惡行。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Hesiod ends by teaching Perses the days Zeus has marked out on the month — folk should know and teach them to their household. The thirtieth day is best for the housekeeper's tasks of meting out and weighing; sacred are the first, the fourth, and the seventh, for on the seventh Leto bore Apollo of the golden sword; the eighth and the ninth are good for opening the jars and for work among men.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 750-780 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: Around the calendar he hangs a body of household taboo: wash your hands before you pour the dark wine to Zeus, or the god will not heed your prayers when you call; never urinate standing toward the sun, nor on the road of wayfarers, nor in a river; do not cross a shining stream with hands and guilt unstained, for the gods visit it with pain; never leave the mixing-bowl and the cup at once, nor the ladle in the bowl — fatal blend; get no twelve-year-old boy to sit upon the funeral mound; nor will a widow's water-jar serve for washings without penalty. For so it is that even small talk is holy among the gods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 724-752 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: Under all runs one doctrine: men's sins bring their own revenge. When one does harm to a beggar's suppliant or to his guest, or, wrapt in shamelessness, goes in to his brother's wife or the mother's orphan child, or rails at the father old upon his sorrowful bed, and gives offence to the gods, then at once the avenging judges watch. Zeus, they warn, has thirty thousand immortal watchers: watchers of divisions and judgments all over the earth, clothed in the mist of air, ever looking upon men's wrongful doings — and the eye of Zeus, they say, notes all and does not accidentally miss.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 250-280, 750-759 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

title.en: The Short Road Down and the Long Road Up

region.zh: 波厄提亞阿斯克拉村（象徵性定位）

source.work: Hesiod, Works and Days, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White (1914), lines ca. 287-320

summary.en: Hesiod sketches the two roads a man can walk: wickedness is close, flat, and easy to take in armfuls; the gods have set the road to virtue on the opposite side — long, uphill, rough at first, but easy once you stand on the summit. He grades three kinds of men by how they grasp the future, and warns Perses that Hunger walks close behind the idle.
summary.zh: 赫西俄德描畫兩條路：作惡之路近在咫尺，平坦易行，線路可大量批取；而眾神把通向德行的路置於其上——漫長、陡峭、開端崎嶇，但登頂之後反覺輕鬆。他依「如何對待未來」把人分為三等，並警告佩耳塞斯：懶惰者身旁總跟著飢餓。

sensitivity.note: Ancient literary source; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Hesiod gave Perses rules for good living, and drew the map of conduct as two roads. The way to wickedness is short and smooth: she lives just around the corner, and you can take her in armfuls. But between us and goodness the immortal gods have set sweat: the road to virtue is long and climbs, rough at the top of the climb; yet once a man stands at the summit, easy becomes the going.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 287-295 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: He then rated mankind by its use of the future: that man is best of all who takes thought for his own affairs, weighing how the later thing shall come out best; good also is he who takes another's advice; but a man with no wits about him, who neither plans nor listens, is useless, pointless as chaff.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 295-315 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: And the wages of each road are plain. Do the work the gods have cut out for you, and lay it up safely; contentious Perses must work with boldness, so that Hunger come not and Demeter be glad: the man who labours finds the barn full of Demeter's grain; the idle man has Hunger close at hand — the gods and men alike despise him, a stingless drone that eats the toil of the bees. Work is no shame; it is the idle man who eats his shame.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 315-320 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

region.zh: 波厄提亞阿斯克拉村（象徵性定位）

source.work: Hesiod, Works and Days, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White (1914), lines ca. 11-41

summary.en: Opening his case against Perses, Hesiod distinguishes two goddesses both called Strife: one cruel, fosterer of battle, whom no man loves; the other set by Zeus in the roots of the earth, the elder daughter of Night, who rouses even the lazy to work and is good for men. He tells his brother to choose only the second strife — the healthy envy that fills barns — and not the court-hall quarrels of ruined men.
summary.zh: 赫西俄德向佩耳塞斯陳情：世上原不止一種紛爭女神。其一殘忍好戰，人皆厭之；另一是黑夜的長女，宙斯親置於大地之根，專激懶人上進，對人有益。他勸弟弟只取後者——催人耕作、盈滿穀倉的良性競爭，別再去衙門打那傾家蕩產的官司。

passages.text: Hesiod began his teaching to Perses by correcting a common belief: there is not one Strife in the world, but two goddesses wearing the same name. One is heavy and hateful, fosters evil war and battle, and no man loves her — yet, by the will of the deathless gods, mortals are forced to pay her their honours.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 11-17 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: The other Strife is the elder daughter of dark Night; Zeus, who dwells in the aether, set her in the roots of the earth, and she is far kinder to men. She stirs the sluggish to labour: a man who notices his neighbour growing rich hurries to plough, to plant, to set his house in order — potter strives with potter, craftsman with craftsman, beggar envies beggar, and minstrel envies minstrel. This Strife, the poet says, is wholesome for men.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 17-25 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.

passages.text: So Perses must not let the god-hated Strife drag his heart from work while he lounges about listening to quarrels at the courthouse. He reminds his brother: you had no livelihood, and so wrangled; but that grain-store is the true prize — lay it up betimes, so that you need not go bothering others, for friends may tide you over once or twice, but not for ever; third appeal answers nothing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Works and Days, lines ca. 25-35 (Evelyn-White 1914); not verbatim.
